content: Patients should have their complete blood count (CBC) and a chemistry profile checked periodically to monitor for any potential adverse effects or abnormalities. There is limited information available regarding the intravenous (IV) compatibility of tolmetin in the drug label. In the event of an overdose, the stomach should be emptied either by inducing vomiting or performing gastric lavage, followed by the administration of activated charcoal to reduce absorption of the drug. The mechanism of action of tolmetin sodium is not fully understood. However, studies in laboratory animals and humans have demonstrated that its anti-inflammatory effects are not due to stimulation of the pituitary-adrenal axis. Tolmetin sodium inhibits prostaglandin synthetase in vitro and reduces plasma levels of prostaglandin E in humans. This reduction in prostaglandin synthesis may be responsible for its anti-inflammatory effects. Tolmetin sodium does not appear to alter the course of the underlying disease in humans. Studies in animals have shown that tolmetin sodium possesses anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic properties. In rats, tolmetin sodium prevents the development of experimentally induced polyarthritis and reduces established inflammation. Each tolmetin sodium capsule, intended for oral administration, contains 492 mg of tolmetin sodium (as the dihydrate), equivalent to 400 mg of tolmetin. Each capsule also contains 36 mg (1.568 mEq) of sodium and the following inactive ingredients: FD&C Red No. 3, FD&C Yellow No. 6, gelatin, magnesium stearate, pregelatinized starch, talc, and titanium dioxide. Each tolmetin sodium tablet, intended for oral administration, contains 246 mg of tolmetin sodium (as the dihydrate), equivalent to 200 mg of tolmetin. Each tablet also contains 18 mg (0.784 mEq) of sodium and the following inactive ingredients: magnesium stearate, microcrystalline cellulose, pregelatinized starch, sodium starch glycolate, and talc. The pKa of tolmetin is 3.5, and tolmetin sodium is freely soluble in water. Tolmetin sodium is classified as a nonselective nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). There is limited information available regarding the pharmacodynamics of tolmetin in the drug label. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis and in healthy volunteers, tolmetin sodium is rapidly and almost completely absorbed, with peak plasma levels reached within 30 to 60 minutes after an oral therapeutic dose. Controlled studies have shown that the time to reach peak plasma concentration is approximately 20 minutes longer when a 600 mg tablet is administered compared to an equivalent dose given as 200 mg tablets. The clinical significance of this finding, if any, is unknown. Tolmetin exhibits biphasic elimination from the plasma, consisting of a rapid phase with a half-life of 1 to 2 hours, followed by a slower phase with a half-life of approximately 5 hours. Peak plasma levels of approximately 40 µg/mL are achieved with a 400 mg oral dose. Nearly all of the administered dose is recovered in the urine within 24 hours, either as an inactive oxidative metabolite or as conjugates of tolmetin. An 18-day multiple-dose study demonstrated no accumulation of tolmetin when compared with a single dose. In two fecal blood loss studies of 4 to 6 days' duration involving 15 subjects each, tolmetin sodium did not induce an increase in blood loss compared to the drug-free control period. In the same studies, aspirin caused greater blood loss than observed during the drug-free control period and greater blood loss than during the tolmetin sodium treatment period. In one of the two studies, indomethacin caused greater fecal blood loss than during the drug-free control period; in the second study, indomethacin did not induce a significant increase in blood loss. Tolmetin sodium is effective in treating both acute flares and in the long-term management of symptoms associated with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis, tolmetin sodium is as effective as aspirin and indomethacin in controlling disease activity. However, the frequency of milder gastrointestinal adverse effects and tinnitus was lower in tolmetin-treated patients compared to those treated with aspirin, and the incidence of central nervous system adverse effects was lower compared to indomethacin-treated patients. In patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, tolmetin sodium is as effective as aspirin in controlling disease activity, with a similar incidence of adverse reactions. Mean serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT) values, initially elevated in patients on prior aspirin therapy, remained elevated in the aspirin group but decreased in the tolmetin sodium group. Tolmetin sodium has demonstrated additional therapeutic benefits when added to a regimen of gold salts and, to a lesser extent, with corticosteroids. However, tolmetin sodium should not be used in conjunction with salicylates, as the combination is unlikely to provide greater benefit and may increase the potential for adverse reactions. Long-term studies have shown that tolmetin sodium does not possess carcinogenic potential. A 24-month study in rats at doses up to 75 mg/kg/day and an 18-month study in mice at doses up to 50 mg/kg/day revealed no evidence of carcinogenicity. Additionally, tolmetin sodium showed no mutagenic potential in the Ames Salmonella-Microsomal Activation Test. Reproductive studies revealed no impairment of fertility in animals, although effects on parturition have been observed, as with other prostaglandin inhibitors. Patients should be informed of the potential cardiovascular (CV) risks associated with NSAIDs, including myocardial infarction (MI) or stroke, which may result in hospitalization or death. Patients should be alert to signs and symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or slurred speech, and seek medical advice if these occur. Similarly, patients should be made aware of the potential gastrointestinal (GI) risks, including ulcers and bleeding, which may also result in hospitalization or death. Patients should be vigilant for signs of GI ulceration or bleeding and seek medical attention if these symptoms arise.
